    • New tests: test-assign_sample_sets.R, test-set_validation_behavior.R, plus new cases added to test-get_hoacc.R and test-get_prediction_matrix.R covering the validation-via-sampleAlg path specifically (including the get.prediction.matrix() regression, constructed so it would have failed against the pre-fix redundant-pre-filter code).
  • plot_3d_trajectory() (new) + plot_2d_trajectory() (new) – both in R/plot_3d_trajectory.R, sharing a set of internal helpers. plot_3d_trajectory() was ported in from a user-written analysis script (ColorTriplets/R/ in the data directory) that built a 3-D scatterplot of one query point of a smooth_embedding_trajectory() result, with a gray effective_n density strip along the bottom and a red marker at the point shown – exactly the kind of per-frame visualization needed to animate a trajectory (e.g. via gifski, as discussed earlier for the Gabor-wavelet dataset). scatterplot3d added to Suggests (new dependency; not previously used anywhere in the package). Two real design gaps surfaced and resolved with the user before integrating, not guessed at: (1) the original signature carried n_query/bw parameters that were never referenced anywhere in the function body – confirmed unused, then dropped; (2) pos (participant positions) was also unused in the original, but the user wanted it kept and wired up to plot each participant’s own position as a small black dot along the same bottom strip – implemented via a linear map from range(traj$query_points) onto the strip’s rendered x-extent, verified visually (not just “ran without erroring”): rendered a real plot on icon_emb_ind and confirmed the dots land exactly where separately-traced fraction values say they should (4 clustered near one edge, 2 near the other, matching this bundled dataset’s known small-vs-large participant split established earlier in this doc). Also answered a user question about the cleanest way to pass arbitrary scatterplot3d appearance parameters through: added ..., merged with the function’s own defaults via modifyList() then dispatched with do.call() (so e.g. angle =/grid = can be overridden without the function needing a named parameter for every possibility) – plain ... forwarding alone would have hit “formal argument matched by multiple actual arguments” errors on any of the names already hardcoded internally, which modifyList()-before-do.call() avoids.
    • get_axis_ranges() (computes shared, zero-centered axis limits across every query point so repeated calls at increasing loc don’t rescale frame to frame) needed a na.rm = TRUE fix while porting it in: smooth_embedding_trajectory() can legitimately return an all-NA embedding for a query point with no meaningful kernel weight (its own documented behavior), and the original un-guarded min()/max() calls would have let one such point poison every axis’s range to NA.
    • add_density_to_cube() (kept close to the original) reaches into scatterplot3d’s own internal, non-exported closure variables to find where its 3-D cube actually renders in 2-D plot coordinates, since the package exposes no public API for this – documented clearly as a fragility inherent to the chosen graphics approach, not something with a clean fix available.
    • Immediately after plot_3d_trajectory() was done, the user asked for a 2-D sibling with the same argument conventions (plot_2d_trajectory(), base graphics::plot(), no new dependency). Rather than duplicating the bottom-strip/red-marker/participant-dot logic, refactored first: pulled the strip-drawing math out of add_density_to_cube() into a new add_density_strip(xlim, density, ...) that takes an explicit x-range instead of deriving one from a scatterplot3d object (add_density_to_cube() now just works out that xlim from the cube internals and delegates to it – a 2-D plot’s own x-range is already exactly par("usr")[1:2], no cube-geometry reconstruction needed at all), and pulled the red-marker-plus-participant-dots logic out into add_trajectory_markers(d, traj, pos, loc), used identically by both 2-D and 3-D versions. Also factored out the loc-bounds-checking into validate_traj_loc(), shared the same way. plot_2d_trajectory() needed one thing the 3-D version didn’t: a par(mar = ...) bump for enough bottom-margin room for the strip to render via xpd = TRUE without being clipped at the figure boundary (scatterplot3d() handles its own margin internally via its own mar argument; base plot() has no equivalent, so this function sets it directly) – saved and restored via on.exit() so it doesn’t leak into the caller’s later plots (confirmed with a dedicated test comparing par("mar") before and after). Both new plots verified visually, not just “ran without erroring”: rendered real PNGs on icon_emb_ind and confirmed the strip, red marker, and black participant dots all land in the expected positions in both the 2-D and 3-D cases.
    • All five helpers (get_axis_ranges(), validate_traj_loc(), add_density_strip(), add_density_to_cube(), add_trajectory_markers()) kept internal (not exported), matching this package’s existing convention for small single-purpose supporting functions (e.g. read_raw_data.R’s own internal helpers) – only plot_3d_trajectory()/plot_2d_trajectory() themselves are exported.
  • Real bug found and fixed in add_trajectory_markers() right after the functions above shipped: participant-position dots were essentially invisible. The user reported “it all works without error, but I’m not seeing black dots” even after rendering large. Chased two hypotheses before finding the real one, each tested directly rather than assumed: (1) suspected pos being passed as a raw cmdscale(d, k=1) matrix (confirmed from the user’s real notebook, ColorTriplets/Color_analysis.Rmd: pos <- cmdscale(p1rd, 1), no [,1] extraction – cmdscale() always returns a matrix, even for k=1, a well-known general R gotcha) – reproduced this exact pattern directly, but traced the actual arithmetic step by step (via assignInNamespace()-instrumented debug prints on the real call path, not just an isolated reconstruction) and found the position math was computing correctly regardless, and separately confirmed smooth_embedding_trajectory() itself is also unaffected by a matrix positions argument (identical()-checked every field of a traj built with the matrix against one built with the equivalent vector); (2) the user then asked directly whether the gray density bars might be painted after the dots, hiding them (z-order) – tested this conclusively by manually overdrawing huge, bright magenta markers at the exact same computed coordinates on top of a real rendered plot and confirming they appeared clearly on top, ruling out z-order/clipping entirely. The actual cause: the dots were real, correctly positioned, and correctly drawn on top the whole time – just pch = 20, cex = 0.5, which is too small and low-contrast to reliably spot against the gray density-strip’s own tick-mark-like bars at realistic plot sizes (confirmed by rendering the same real data larger – still essentially unnoticeable). Fixed by bumping the default to pch = 19, cex = 1.1, now clearly visible at normal sizes in both the 2-D and 3-D versions (shared via add_trajectory_markers()). Also kept the matrix-pos defensive fix from hypothesis (1) even though it turned out not to be the actual root cause here: drop(as.matrix(pos)) now silently handles a 1-row or 1-column matrix (the exact cmdscale() mistake) and raises a clear error for a genuine multi-column matrix instead of silently misreading it – a real, confirmed-easy-to-hit foot-gun worth guarding against regardless of whether it was the cause of this particular report. Two new regression tests lock down the matrix-handling behavior specifically.
    • Even after that fix shipped and was reinstalled, the user still reported no dots in their real notebook – every package-level check passed (body(tripletTools:::add_trajectory_markers) showed the fix; par("usr")/manual position math were all correct; xaxt/tick.marks suppression, tested directly, made no difference), yet a trace() placed on add_trajectory_markers() fired only when called manually, never when invoked through a normal top-level plot_3d_trajectory(...) call – the decisive clue that the package’s own exported function was never actually being reached. Root cause: not a package bug at all – RStudio’s default “restore .RData on startup” had reloaded an old global-environment copy of plot_3d_trajectory (originally source()-d from the user’s pre-package standalone script), which R resolves before the package namespace on every bare call, silently shadowing the reinstalled, fixed version with no error or warning of any kind. Resolved by clearing the workspace and re-running cleanly; confirmed fixed by calling the fully-qualified tripletTools::plot_3d_trajectory() directly. General lesson worth remembering for any future “works in my test, not in the user’s session” mismatch: check environment(fn) for unexpected global-env shadowing before assuming the installed package code itself is at fault, especially on a second report after a fix that already checked out correctly in isolation.
  • vignettes/trajectory_vignette.Rmd – new vignette built on top of plot_3d_trajectory()/plot_2d_trajectory()/smooth_embedding_trajectory()/generalized_procrustes() once the dot bug above was fully resolved, directly adapted from the user’s own real analysis notebook (ColorTriplets/Color_analysis.Rmd) rather than written from scratch. Demonstrates treating individual differences as a continuous manifold (as an alternative to the discrete-clustering tools covered in vignette("tripletTools")), using a real dataset chosen specifically because it shows this cleanly in a domain where that kind of heterogeneity might not be expected: 58 color patches, 46 participants, from Zimnicki et al.’s CogSci poster work (unpublished otherwise – https://escholarship.org/uc/item/8778p3t3, cited directly in the new data objects’ @source). New bundled datasets, same icon_* convention (inst/extdata/color_*.csv -> data-raw/color_triplets.R/data-raw/color_embeddings.R -> data/*.rda, see “Data objects” above): color_triplets (340KB compressed, the largest triplet dataset bundled so far – 46 participants vs. icon_triplets’ 6 – checked compression first rather than assuming it’d be fine, since the raw CSV is ~30x icon_all_triplets.csv‘s size), color_emb_ind, color_emb_group, and a genuinely new kind of object for this package, color_lab (the patches’ own CIE LAB coordinates – not a fitted embedding, a reference point for comparison). Caught a real, easy-to-miss correctness bug while building this, before it reached the vignette: confirmed directly (not assumed) that color_lab and color_emb_group/color_emb_ind are not stored in the same row order, which would have silently misaligned items in any row-positional comparison (e.g. vegan::procrustes(), which matches configurations by row position, not rowname) – the vignette always re-indexes by rowname first (color_lab[rownames(color_emb_group), ]), and this is called out explicitly in color_lab’s own roxygen docs as a standing gotcha for this specific pair of objects. Every number and figure in the vignette was independently computed and visually inspected (rendered PNGs read directly) before being written into the prose, not assumed from the analogous real notebook – this surfaced one genuine, interesting result worth noting for its own sake: estimate_intrinsic_dimension() on the participant representational-distance matrix comes back forced_to_one = TRUE, which is exactly the documented false-negative pattern from that function’s own history (dominance ratio ~4.9x) rather than a genuine absence of structure, and the vignette uses this as a live, real-data example of that exact documented caveat rather than inventing a synthetic one. The final payoff figure (held-out validation accuracy from the two ends of the smoothed manifold, plotted against each participant’s own manifold position) shows a clean, strong crossover (R² = 0.70 from a 16-query-point grid) – confirmed visually before writing it up, not just from the regression number alone. Vignette verified end-to-end via rmarkdown::render() (all 27 chunks, no errors/warnings) with output read back and spot-checked against the independently-computed values. Added to the vignette list in README.md and the Repository layout section above.
    • Real bug the user caught after reading the rendered vignette, not caught by my own verification pass: the two “True LAB” panels under “Does the group embedding recover real color space?” had visibly shuffled colors relative to the identical-data panels one section above. Root cause: pcols had been derived once from color_lab’s own row order (correct for the first section, which plots color_lab directly), then reused in the next chunk against lab_matched/aligned, which are in color_emb_group’s different row order – the alignment math itself was correctly row-matched (verified separately beforehand), but the bg = plotting color for each point was not. Checking afterward turned up the same risk a second place: plot_3d_trajectory(traj, pos, loc = i, pcols = pcols, ...) in the trajectory-grid section also needs pcols in embedding order (traj$embeddings[[i]] preserves color_emb_ind/color_emb_group’s row order, confirmed directly), which it happened to already be, but only by accident of chunk ordering, not by design. Fixed properly rather than patched per-chunk: confirmed all embedding-side objects (color_emb_group, every color_emb_ind[[i]]) already share one identical row order, so the vignette now establishes pcols <- rownames(color_emb_group) exactly once near the top and re-indexes color_lab to match it at that same point (lab_matched <- color_lab[pcols, ]), with every later chunk reusing those same two objects rather than re-deriving row order locally. Re-rendered and re-verified by extracting the embedded PNGs straight out of the rendered HTML (base64-decoded) and visually confirming the previously-mismatched panels now exactly match, and that the trajectory-grid colors cohere into a smooth gradient around the final ring frame. Worth remembering generally: verifying that an alignment/statistical computation used correctly row-matched inputs is not the same check as verifying every plot built from its output used a color/label vector in that same row order – these are separate things to check, and only the rendered figure actually catches the latter.
  • run_embeddings_from_list()/run_embeddings() gained a compute_group argument (default TRUE, preserving prior behavior) letting a caller skip the group-level embedding entirely when only the per-participant ones are needed. Threaded through all three layers of the pipeline: inst/python/compute_embeddings.py::process_all_workers() gained the actual compute_group parameter and now wraps its whole “Group-level embedding across all workers” block (including the embeddings_group.csv write and the "group" model_history/embeddings row) in if compute_group: rather than running it unconditionally; run_embeddings() (R) passes the flag straight through to that Python call; run_embeddings_from_list() (R) passes it through again and, when FALSE, sets group = NULL directly rather than trying to extract a "group" row that was never written (which would otherwise silently produce a zero-row matrix instead of a clear NULL). Verified live, not just by reading the code: ran the real Python backend (available in this dev environment) with compute_group = FALSE and confirmed from the actual training log that “Processing group-level embedding across all workers…” never printed for that run, while it did for an otherwise-identical default (compute_group = TRUE) run just before and after it in the same test session. New regression test (test-run_embeddings_from_list.R) checks res$group is NULL, no "group" row in res$history, and embeddings_group.csv isn’t written to output_dir.
  • Real, pre-existing bug found and fixed: seed never actually controlled individual/group embedding fits in run_embeddings_from_list()/run_embeddings()/run_group_embedding_from_list(). Surfaced when the user reported that a real dataset fit with compute_group = FALSE came out “much worse” than a prior run, and asked for the recently-revised code to be double-checked before spending a long re-fit to isolate the cause. Diff inspection first ruled out compute_group itself: the per-worker fitting loop in process_all_workers() is byte-for-byte unchanged by that commit, and the (now-optional) group fit always runs strictly after the entire per-worker loop finishes, so it cannot feed back into individual fits either way. Confirmed this empirically too, not just by reading the diff – a quick synthetic-data check showed compute_group = TRUE vs FALSE gave different individual embeddings even with the same seed, which led to the real root cause: a control test with identical arguments (same compute_group, same seed) on two separate calls also gave different embeddings. Traced directly: train_embedding_model() only seeds numpy/torch when its own random_state argument is non-None (if random_state is not None: np.random.seed(...); torch.manual_seed(...)), but process_all_workers()’s per-worker loop and group-fitting block never passed random_state at all – always None. Meanwhile run_embeddings()’s R-level seed argument only called random$seed(as.integer(seed)), seeding Python’s built-in random module, which train_embedding_model() never reads (confirmed random is imported in compute_embeddings.py but never actually called anywhere in the file). So seed was a complete no-op for fit reproducibility the whole time – two calls with identical arguments could, and did, produce meaningfully different embeddings purely from uncontrolled weight initialization, independent of any data or code change. The exact same gap existed in the sibling function run_group_embedding_from_list(): it called set.seed(seed) (R-level only) but never passed random_state to its own train_embedding() call either, even though train_embedding() already supports random_state correctly (confirmed by checking that function’s own tests, which explicitly reproduce embeddings via it) – fixed by following that exact already-working pattern, rather than inventing a new one.
    • Fix, threaded through properly rather than patched at one layer: process_all_workers() (Python) gained a seed=None parameter; each worker now gets random_state = seed + worker_index (0-based position among df['worker_id'].unique(), stable since the input CSV’s row order comes directly from triplet_list’s own R list order) and the group fit (if computed) gets seed + len(unique_worker_ids) – one past the last worker index, guaranteed collision-free. run_embeddings() (R) now passes seed = as.integer(seed) through to process_all_workers() and no longer calls the dead random$seed()/reticulate::import("random") lines at all. run_group_embedding_from_list() now passes random_state = as.integer(seed) to its train_embedding() call (its pre-existing set.seed(seed) is left in place, since that still legitimately controls the R-level sample() shuffle used in its 70/30 train/test fallback path).
    • Verified live, not just by reading the fix: re-ran the exact control test that exposed the bug (identical arguments, two separate calls) and confirmed identical() now holds for every participant’s embedding and the group embedding; confirmed a different seed still gives a different embedding (not a degenerate always-the-same-output bug); re-ran the compute_group = TRUE vs FALSE comparison with the fix in place and confirmed individual embeddings are now identical() regardless of the flag, closing the loop on the user’s original report. The duplicate-training-curve evidence is visible directly in the test-run log ([early stop] loss/accuracy trajectories repeating verbatim across two “same seed” calls). New regression tests in test-run_embeddings_from_list.R and test-run_group_embedding_from_list.R lock all of this down; the latter’s existing norm_penalty test had its own comment documenting the then-known “runs aren’t reproducible enough to compare” limitation, now stale and removed.
    • Open question the user’s original report leaves unresolved: whether their perceived “much worse” embeddings were entirely explained by this pre-existing non-determinism, or whether their own acknowledged test/validation-trial treatment changes also contributed. With seed now actually working, re-running their real dataset with a fixed seed (with and without their data changes) would cleanly separate the two – not yet done, since it requires their real, slow-to-fit dataset.
  • plot_pics() fixed to preserve each image’s own native pixel aspect ratio, instead of stretching it to match the plotting surface’s. Root cause: the old sizing code computed xsz <- psize * xrange and ysz <- psize * yrange independently from the axis data ranges alone – working out the actual physical box size this produces (via par('pin'), the plot region’s size in inches) shows the rendered box’s physical width/height ratio always equals pin[1]/pin[2] (the plotting region’s own aspect ratio), regardless of the image’s own shape – so any non-square plotting window (the common case – e.g. png(width=, height=) with unequal width/height) silently stretched every image to match the window, not just unusual cases. Fixed by anchoring psize to physical height only (psize * pin[2], unchanged in spirit from before) and deriving the box’s width from the image’s own native aspect ratio (dim(currpic)[2]/dim(currpic)[1], works for both PNG arrays and "raster" matrices) combined with the actual data-units-per-inch conversion in each direction – factored into a new internal (non-exported) helper, compute_pic_halfsize(native_ar, psize, pin, xlim, ylim), deliberately taking pin/xlim/ylim as plain arguments rather than reading par() itself so it’s unit-testable without a live graphics device. Verified algebraically (worked through by hand before implementing, confirming the new formula reduces to the exact old one when both the image and the plotting device are square) and empirically: tests/testthat/test-plot_pics.R checks the physical aspect ratio comes out correct for a square image on a non-square device and for a non-square (2:1) image on a non-square device with non-square axis ranges, plus a real rendered check on icon_pics at an extreme 1400x500 (2.8:1) device confirming the icons render square and undistorted, where they’d have been visibly squished under the old code.
  • assign_sample_sets() changed from an independent per-trial coin-flip to an exact per-participant count, at the user’s request. Previously sampleAlg == "random" trials were each independently assigned to test via runif(n()) <= test_prop, so the number of test trials per participant only matched test_prop in expectation – two participants with the same number of random trials could (and typically did) end up with different test-set sizes. Now a new internal (non-exported) helper, select_test_trials(), computes n_test = round(test_prop * n_random) once per participant and selects exactly that many random trials (via sample.int(n_random, n_test), without replacement) to be test – so same trial count always means same test count, and different trial counts still get matched proportions with a controlled, deterministic-given-seed exact count. Kept the existing case_when()/group_by(worker_id) structure, just swapped the random-trial branch’s condition for a call to the new helper (computed in a { } block inside the single mutate() call, so the intermediate logical vector doesn’t leak out as a stray column). Verified the existing claim in this function’s own docs still holds after the change – validation trials still never consume any of test_prop’s random draws, since select_test_trials() only looks at sampleAlg == "random" rows and runs identically regardless of validation_mode – and added new regression tests locking down the exact-count property directly (same n_random -> same test count across participants; round()’s exact behavior at a non-round test_prop * n_random; the test_prop ∈ {0, 1} extremes; a zero-random-trials participant not erroring).
  • loo_trajectory_accuracy() (new) – fixes a second, independently real data-leakage bug in the smooth_embedding_trajectory() prediction workflow, found by the user noticing an apparent contradiction: test_dominant_dimension() gave a non-significant p (~0.1) on a real dataset where PC1 explained only ~9% of variance (dominance_ratio ~2, matched almost exactly to this function’s own validated “weak, correctly-not-detected” synthetic case), yet the user’s own crossover-prediction analysis (left-end/right-end smoothed embeddings predicting held-out judgments) showed a strong, clean crossover – which the user read as evidence test_dominant_dimension() was underpowered/wrong.
    • Root cause, confirmed empirically rather than argued theoretically: smooth_embedding_trajectory()’s kernel weighting gives “no participant’s weight ever exactly zero” (its own pre-existing docs) – so a participant near the left end of the manifold contributes, with real weight, to the very left-end smoothed embedding later evaluated against their own held-out judgments. A participant’s own fitted embedding unsurprisingly predicts their own behavior better than a random other participant’s would, regardless of whether any genuine cross-participant structure exists at all – so the crossover test as commonly used (compute the trajectory once on everyone, then evaluate each participant against their nearest query point) cannot distinguish “real shared structure with actual neighbors” from “trivial self-contribution.” Demonstrated directly: a synthetic dataset of participants with fully independent, unrelated true embeddings (zero real structure, by construction) produced a strong, “significant”-looking crossover (R-squared 0.27, p = 0.003) under the naive approach – collapsing to non-significance (R-squared 0.06, p = 0.18) once each participant was excluded from just the smoothing step, and to near-zero (R-squared 0.004, p = 0.80) once fully excluded, including from the 1-D axis computation itself (the stricter version this function implements).
    • What it does: for every participant, drops them entirely (from dist_mat before cmdscale computes the 1-D axis, and from elist before smooth_embedding_trajectory() refits the trajectory on the remaining n-1), then evaluates their held-out trials (trialtype, typically "validation") against every one of n_query query points along that fully out-of-sample trajectory – giving an n x n_query accuracy matrix per participant, rather than one number per participant at whichever single query point happened to be nearest them. Returns query_points and effective_n per participant too (these shift slightly participant to participant, since each leave-one-out fit spans a slightly different (n-1)-participant range), plus full_sample_position (each participant’s position from the full, non-leave-one-out sample) for context/plotting only – never used in any prediction.
    • get.rep.dist()’s pairwise distances were confirmed (read directly, not assumed) to depend only on the two participants in each cell – so subsetting the already-computed dist_mat per left-out participant is exactly equivalent to recomputing get.rep.dist() from scratch on the remaining participants, no expensive distance recomputation needed.
    • smooth_embedding_trajectory()’s own roxygen gained a new warning section () pointing to this function, so the pitfall is documented where someone would naturally first encounter the tool that has it, not only here.
    • Resolved (numbers below superseded two bullets down, once the bundled color_emb_ind data itself turned out to be stale): vignettes/trajectory_vignette.Rmd re-verified with loo_trajectory_accuracy() and fixed. The crossover section now explicitly explains the leakage pitfall in prose (not just a passing mention) before showing the corrected analysis, since this is exactly the kind of mistake a reader could otherwise repeat.
  • test_dominant_dimension() (new) + integration into estimate_intrinsic_dimension() (new dominance_p_value, test_dominance/n_simulations args) – a direct, simulation-based statistical test for exactly the weakness estimate_intrinsic_dimension()’s own docs already flagged (Horn’s PA conservatism at rank 1, previously only hinted at via the dominance_ratio heuristic). Motivated by the user noticing the same pattern across several real datasets: forced_to_one = TRUE with a clearly dominant leading eigenvalue (4x+ the rest), wanting something more statistically justified than a ratio heuristic.
    • Two earlier designs were tried and both failed real validation, not shipped: (1) bootstrap-eigenvector-stability (Jackson 1993; Peres-Neto, Jackson & Somers 2003/2005 – genuine precedent, verified via search, for testing PCA axis stability under bootstrap resampling) – failed because estimate_intrinsic_dimension()’s coords come from cmdscale(), which is already orthogonal by construction, so re-eigendecomposing bootstrap-resampled copies of it just rediscovers whichever column has the most variance regardless of whether that dominance is real or sampling noise; three variants (direct, correlation-standardized, full cmdscale-refit-per-bootstrap-draw) were tried and all three gave statistically indistinguishable “stability” for genuine synthetic structure vs. pure noise in controlled tests. (2) The literal asymptotic Tracy-Widom distribution (Johnstone 2001; Patterson, Price & Reich 2006) – ruled out before implementing, via a literature check confirming its accuracy is well documented to degrade “when either the sample size or dimension is not too large” – exactly this package’s regime (participant counts in the tens, not thousands).
    • What actually worked, found by going back to Horn’s own original 1965 parallel-analysis proposal (simulated random data) rather than the permutation variant of Buja & Eyuboglu (1992) that estimate_intrinsic_dimension() already implements – but with two modifications that were necessary, confirmed by testing, not assumed: simulating the null at equal variance across candidate dimensions (not matched to the observed data’s own per-dimension variances, which is what both Horn’s original method and permutation do, and is exactly what reintroduces the “beat a shuffled/simulated version of itself” problem for a dominant first axis), and testing the scale-invariant proportion of variance explained by the dimension in question rather than raw eigenvalue magnitude (needed since the observed data and a unit-variance null simulation aren’t otherwise on comparable scales). This is a specific combination this package arrived at via testing, not a direct implementation of any one cited paper’s exact method – documented as such in the function’s own roxygen rather than overclaiming precedent.
    • Validated directly before shipping (own @section Validation, and locked into the test suite): Type I error close to nominal at n = 6, 20, and 30 (observed false-positive rates 4.7-8.7% at alpha = 0.05/0.10); correctly non-significant for pure noise and a weak (variance ratio 2) synthetic dominant dimension; correctly significant from ratio >= 5 at both n = 6 and n = 30. On the real icon_emb_ind data (n = 6, dominance_ratio 5.64), gives p = 0.38 – an honest “can’t distinguish from noise at this sample size” rather than a false positive, illustrating that a large dominance_ratio alone is not sufficient evidence at very small n.
    • estimate_intrinsic_dimension() calls test_dominant_dimension() directly (rank 1) rather than inlining/sharing loop state with its own permutation test, since the new test’s simulation is entirely independent of Horn’s permutation null – simpler and no real efficiency cost. test_dominance = TRUE is the new default (backward-compatible return shape: existing callers just get one new always-present dominance_p_value field, NA when test_dominance = FALSE).
  • Real data-quality bug in the bundled color_emb_ind dataset: it was fit with validation trials leaking into training, making every test_dominant_dimension()/loo_trajectory_accuracy() number already shipped in trajectory_vignette.Rmd wrong. Surfaced when the user ran test_dominant_dimension(p1rd) in their own, independently-refit notebook (ColorTriplets/Color_analysis.Rmd) and got p ≈ 0.09, sharply different from the vignette’s reported p = 0.001. The user’s own diagnosis: “I think in the older version the validation trials had been included when fitting embeddings… I recomputed everything after setting validation trials to ‘holdout’.” Confirmed precisely rather than taken on faith, three ways: (1) table(sampleAlg, sampleSet) on the bundled color_triplets.csv showed all 3864 validation trials at sampleSet = "train" – consistent with, though not proof of, leakage at fit time (triplets CSVs always show this regardless of holdout status, since set_validation_behavior()’s "holdout" setting is applied in-memory and never written back to disk – the real question is always what sampleSet was at fit time, not what the raw CSV shows); (2) direct md5sum comparison of the bundled inst/extdata/color_embeddings_individual.csv against the user’s current live refit showed genuinely different hashes and different coordinate values for the same worker/item cells; (3) the decisive check – the user’s fitdata_p1_3d.csv (per-fit training/test triplet counts) showed n_train_triplets = 29459 for every individual fit, which is exactly the random-trials-only count with the 3864 validation trials excluded (not 29459+3864 = 33323, which is what leakage would produce) – confirming the user’s current files are the methodologically correct, holdout-respecting fits.
    • Scope was narrower than it first looked. md5sum comparison of all three raw inputs showed the bundled group embedding (color_embeddings_group.csv) and the bundled raw triplets (color_triplets.csv) are byte-identical to the user’s current live files – only the individual embeddings (color_embeddings_individual.csv) were stale. (The group embedding’s n_train_triplets = 29459 in the same fitdata_p1_3d.csv independently confirms it too was already fit correctly, despite its file timestamp looking slightly older than the individual-embeddings refit – timestamps on their own would have been misleading here; the fit-stats count is what actually settles it.) So only color_emb_ind/data/color_emb_ind.rda needed re-bundling, not color_emb_group or color_triplets.
    • Fixed by copying the user’s current ColorTriplets/embeddings/p1_3d_ind.csv over inst/extdata/color_embeddings_individual.csv and re-running data-raw/color_embeddings.R’s individual-embedding block to regenerate data/color_emb_ind.rda. No R/ code changed – this was purely a stale-data problem, confirmed by the full test suite (540 tests) passing unchanged before and after (no test depends on color_emb_ind’s specific values).
    • vignettes/trajectory_vignette.Rmd recomputed end-to-end against the corrected data and rewritten to match, not just patched with new numbers: test_for_clusters()’s Hopkins statistic is now significant (p = 0.021, was non-significant before) while BIC still prefers best_g = 1 – re-framed in prose as exactly the signature a continuous (non-discrete) axis should leave on Hopkins, rather than contradicting the “no discrete subgroups” conclusion. test_dominant_dimension() now gives p = 0.096 (not 0.001) on this dataset – i.e. the color dataset is now itself the “dominance test doesn’t reach significance” case, matching what the user’s own notebook found. loo_trajectory_accuracy()’s crossover R² is 0.638 (not 0.676) but remains highly significant (p = 2.9e-12) and visually clean (re-rendered and inspected directly, not assumed). This produced a better, more honest narrative arc than the stale version had: the vignette now explicitly uses its own test_dominant_dimension() non-result as the motivating tension the leave-one-out behavioral analysis resolves (“a p-value of 0.096 on the geometry alone is not a confident detection… the decisive evidence comes from asking that geometry to actually predict something”), rather than reporting two independently-significant results that happened to agree. Verified via full rmarkdown::render() (27 chunks, no errors) with the rendered crossover figure visually inspected.
    • General lesson distinct from the icon_emb_group rownames fix earlier in this file: that was a format bug caught by code inspection; this was a fit-correctness bug that could only be caught by comparing shipped data against an independently-refit version and checking per-fit training counts – a reminder that bundled “precomputed” data objects can silently drift out of sync with the pipeline code/conventions that produced them, with no test or lint able to catch it automatically.
  • plot_2d_trajectory() gained an explicit mar parameter, fixing a real “can’t control plot margins” report. The user found the function left a lot of whitespace around each panel and was “immune” to par(mar = ...), whether set externally beforehand or passed through .... Root cause: unlike plot_3d_trajectory() (where mar is just one more scatterplot3d::scatterplot3d() argument, already reachable through the existing .../modifyList mechanism), plot_2d_trajectory() set its margin via a hardcoded internal graphics::par(mar = c(6, 4, 2, 2)) call, entirely outside that mechanism – ... only ever reached graphics::plot() (which has no mar argument of its own to receive it), and any external par(mar = ...) the caller had already set was captured and overwritten by that same hardcoded call for the duration of the function (then correctly restored afterward via the existing on.exit() – so it wasn’t a restore bug, the margin was just never settable in the first place). Fixed by promoting the hardcoded value to an explicit mar = c(6, 4, 2, 2) parameter (same default, so existing callers are unaffected) used directly in that par() call. Verified visually, not just by reading the fix: rendered a real 4x4 grid of panels with the default mar (showing the reported excess whitespace) against the same grid with mar = c(2.5, 1, 1, 1) (packing tightly, with the effective_n density strip and red marker still rendering correctly, not clipped).
  • find_frequent_triplets() (new) – for retrofitting a post-hoc validation set onto legacy data collected before the sampleAlg == "validation" convention existed, where every triplet was instead sampled independently at random per participant. The user’s stated question going in was whether this is even feasible, given how fast the number of distinct triplets grows with item count – for a study with only 10 items (10 * choose(9, 2) = 360 distinct Center/{Left, Right} combinations), real cross-participant overlap is plausible even from independent random sampling, unlike larger item sets. Counts, per distinct triplet (identity via make.tripnames(), the same left/right-independent convention make.vmat() uses for genuine validation trials – same Center + same unordered {Left, Right} pair, but a different Center on the same three items is a different question, counted separately), both n_participants (distinct worker_ids who judged it – the primary ranking key) and n_trials (total judgments, which can exceed n_participants if one participant repeats a trial) – kept as two separate columns since “repeated across participants” is what the user actually wants for this purpose, not raw occurrence count, which a single chatty participant could inflate. sampleAlg == "check" rows excluded by default (exclude_check = TRUE). Returns the top n by frequency, with Center/Left/Right columns in test.model()/get.hoacc()-ready format (same first-occurrence-row extraction pattern as make.vmat(), for the same reason: parsing items back out of the joined triplet-name string is ambiguous when item names themselves contain underscores). Deliberately does not itself compute a majority-vote Answer for the surfaced triplets (unlike make.vmat()) – that requires first deciding on a frequency/participant threshold using the counts this function returns, which is exactly the judgment call the user was trying to make feasibility of in the first place.
    • Real-data sanity check, not just synthetic unit tests: ran it on the already-bundled icon_triplets, which (being a modern dataset) already has genuine sampleAlg == "validation" trials with a known ground truth – a strong, free correctness check, since the function’s own output can be compared directly against trials already known to be deliberately repeated. Found something genuinely informative in the process: icon_triplets’ own validation set turns out not to be uniformly administered to all 6 participants – of 40 nominal validation triplets, 20 were judged by exactly 5 of 6 participants and 20 by only 1 (confirmed directly, not assumed, by checking a singleton’s raw rows: no other participant has any trial on that same 3-item set, under any Center assignment, so it isn’t a counted-separately center-swap hiding elsewhere – it’s a genuine one-off). find_frequent_triplets(icon_triplets, n = 20) recovers exactly those 20 five-participant triplets, confirmed via exact set equality against the ground truth computed independently from sampleAlg == "validation" – locked into the test suite as a real-data regression test, not just the synthetic small-list cases.
  • assign_validation_from_frequency() (new) – companion to find_frequent_triplets(), the other half of retrofitting a post-hoc validation set onto legacy data: takes its (already-thresholded) candidate output and promotes every matching trial’s sampleAlg to "validation", deliberately not touching sampleSet (that’s set_validation_behavior()’s job, recommended as the natural next call in the docs rather than duplicated here). The user explicitly asked for design recommendations on two open questions: what counts as “often enough,” and how to cap how many of one participant’s own trials get promoted. Resolved both by not owning the frequency threshold at all – find_frequent_triplets() already exists specifically so a caller inspects its n_participants column and decides a threshold deliberately (docs here suggest >= 5 as a reasonable starting point, matching the ballpark this package’s own real bundled validation sets reach, but explicit that it depends on sample size) – and by adding max_per_participant (default Inf, i.e. no cap, since guessing a number without knowing a given study’s typical trial count would be worse than not capping at all) with concrete sizing guidance (~5-10% of a participant’s total trials) rather than a silently-opinionated default.
    • Three real design decisions, each resolved by reasoning about what the cap is for rather than by what was simplest to implement: (1) the cap counts distinct triplets, not raw rows – if a participant happened to judge the same candidate triplet twice (triplets are sampled independently at random in exactly the legacy data this targets, so repeats do happen), both trials are promoted together or not at all, since splitting such a pair would silently destroy exactly the kind of repeated-trial self-consistency data make.vmat()’s own docs call out as valuable. (2) which triplets get dropped once a participant exceeds the cap is controlled by freq_triplets’ own row order – since find_frequent_triplets() already returns candidates sorted by decreasing cross-participant frequency, a chatty participant who matches many candidates keeps the ones shared with the most other participants by default, which is also exactly what you want for the resulting validation set’s own majority votes to be well-supported (rather than, say, picking arbitrarily and ending up with a validation set that’s broad for one participant but thin everywhere else). (3) trials already marked sampleAlg == "check" are never promoted, checked per-row regardless of whether their triplet happens to appear in freq_triplets (defensive against find_frequent_triplets(..., exclude_check = FALSE) having let a check-trial-derived triplet into the candidate set in the first place).
    • Verified end-to-end, not just unit-tested in isolation: built a synthetic 8-participant/10-item “legacy” dataset (fully independent per-participant random sampling, no deliberate repetition – mirroring the user’s real scenario) and confirmed real cross-participant overlap does emerge from chance alone at this item count (up to 6/8 participants sharing a triplet purely coincidentally), that the per-participant cap is respected exactly, that repeated-trial pairs are never split by it, that check trials are never touched, and – the real litmus test – that the promoted result composes correctly with the existing pipeline: set_validation_behavior(result, "holdout") correctly sets sampleSet <- NA only for the newly-promoted trials, and get.hoacc(emb, ..., trialtype = "validation") runs cleanly against the result exactly as it would for genuine, deliberately-collected validation trials.
  • Real, pre-existing bug found and fixed in make.tripnames() – broke on any dataset where Center/Left/Right are integer item indices rather than string item codes, not just a find_frequent_triplets() problem. Surfaced when the user ran find_frequent_triplets() on a real 73-participant dataset and got Error in 1:nitems : argument of length 0. Root cause, confirmed by direct reproduction rather than guessed from reading the code: opts <- as.matrix(tripdat[c("Left","Right")]) produces an integer matrix when Left/Right are integer columns (as they are in this dataset – items coded as raw numeric indices, a legitimate, supported way to identify items that just happened never to have been exercised against this function before); the next line, gsub(" ","",opts), requires character input, and R’s implicit as.character() coercion of a matrix argument silently drops its dim attribute, flattening it to a plain vector – confirmed directly with a minimal repro (gsub(" ","", matrix(1:4,2,2)) returns a dim-less character vector). dim(opts)[1] then evaluates to NULL, and 1:NULL is exactly what throws “argument of length 0”. This affects make.vmat() too (built directly on make.tripnames()), not just the new function that happened to surface it – fixed at the source rather than patched locally. Fix: mode(opts) <- "character" (an in-place type coercion that preserves dim, unlike as.character()) before the gsub() call; also made the Center coercion explicit (as.character(tripdat$Center)) for consistency, though that line was never actually broken (vectors have no dim to lose). New regression test in test-make_tripnames.R locks down the exact failure mode (multi-row integer-coded Center/Left/Right, which is what actually exercises dim(opts)[1] > 1; a single-row case wouldn’t have caught this). Verified against a reconstruction of the user’s actual scenario (73 participants, 10 items, integer item codes, ~100 random trials each): find_frequent_triplets() now runs cleanly and finds real, strong cross-participant overlap (up to 28/73 participants sharing a triplet) – confirming the user’s original premise (small item counts make post-hoc validation-set construction from purely-random legacy sampling genuinely viable) actually holds once this bug is out of the way.
  • make.vmat() gained n/nmaj/p/sig columns, at the user’s request, directly automating the manual binomial sanity-check they’d already been doing by hand in their own notebook (the Gabor exp1 analysis: “For 38 participants, 25 or more agreeing with the majority is unlikely to occur by chance (p < 0.04)”). n and nmaj are just the numerator/denominator already computed inside the existing per-triplet loop (sum(thisone)/max(thisone)), newly exposed as their own columns; p is the one-sided binomial p-value for observing nmaj or more agreements out of n under a p = 0.5 chance-guessing null (stats::pbinom(nmaj - 1, n, 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE), vectorized across all triplets after the loop rather than folded into it) – 0.5 specifically because each judgment is a forced binary choice between two options, so pure guessing is 50/50 by construction, not because the two options are assumed equally likely to be the “true” answer for other reasons. sig is simply p < 0.05. Verified the p-value formula two ways: it matches stats::binom.test(nmaj, n, p = 0.5, alternative = "greater")$p.value exactly for a representative row (now locked into the test suite), and reproduces the user’s own by-hand number precisely (pbinom(24, 38, 0.5, lower.tail = FALSE) = 0.0365, consistent with their “p < 0.04” claim). Explicitly documented in the function’s own roxygen that sig is not a meaningful filter at very low n – a triplet with only 1-2 judgments can never reach significance regardless of outcome (Binomial(1, 0.5) tops out at p = 0.5) – illustrated live in overview_vignette.Rmd‘s existing validation-agreement section using icon_triplets’ own real split (20 triplets with a single judgment, all non-significant by construction; of the 20 triplets with 5 judgments each, 11 reach significance), verified by actually rendering the vignette rather than assuming the added chunk’s output. New columns are purely additive – inserted after the existing pmaj column and before the already-appended Center/Left/Right block, so the existing positional test (vmat[[1]][1,3] for pmaj) was unaffected and needed no change.
  • The pkgdown GitHub Actions build broke on push, right after trajectory_vignette.Rmd was committed – found via the GitHub Actions REST API (not the HTML page – gh CLI isn’t installed here) after the user reported it, then reproduced and confirmed fixed with a real local pkgdown::build_site_github_pages(new_process = FALSE, install = FALSE) run rather than guessing from the log alone. Root cause: _pkgdown.yml keeps an explicit articles:/navbar listing of every vignette (see its own in-file comment on why – needed for the navbar dropdown to show individual links rather than collapsing to one “Articles” entry), and pkgdown’s own sitrep check treats any vignette missing from that list as a hard build failure (“1 vignette missing from index”), not a warning – a new vignette that’s never added to _pkgdown.yml breaks every subsequent push’s pkgdown build, silently from the vignette-author’s point of view (nothing about writing or committing the .Rmd itself fails). Fixed by adding trajectory_vignette to both the articles.contents list and the navbar.components.articles.menu list in _pkgdown.yml, positioned to match the order already used in README.md. General lesson: adding a new vignette to this package means a fourth file, not three – the .Rmd itself, README.md’s list, and this file’s Repository layout section were all updated for trajectory_vignette.Rmd, but _pkgdown.yml was missed; check all four together from now on whenever a vignette is added.
  • Recalibrated recovery_sweep_params_template.yml’s max_epochs after 0bc1af7’s dead-tolerance fix (see that commit’s own message for the bug itself). The original 60000/3000 calibration had been run against the buggy early-stopping check, so it wasn’t actually measuring genuine convergence – rerunning the same two worst-offending cells (fit_alpha=0.1/0.5, same ground-truth/triplet/fit seeds) against the fixed code at the real deployed tol_window=3000/tolerance=1e-4 gave genuinely-converged stopping points of ~60750 and ~89670 epochs respectively – both far below the >161000/200000+ the pre-fix bug had implied were needed, and close enough to the original 60000 ceiling to confirm that ceiling was already roughly right once the stopping rule actually worked. max_epochs raised to 120000 (comfortable headroom above the observed worst case) rather than anything near the pre-fix numbers; higher fitting-alphas were already converging well under 60000 in the original deployment (epoch-ceiling hit rate 63% at alpha=2 down to 4.4% at alpha=Inf, vs. 90%+ at alpha<=0.5), so this mainly gives the slow cells room to finish without meaningfully raising the sweep’s total cost. General lesson: when a single early-stopping/convergence calibration run looks surprisingly bad (here: a fit needing 2-3x the expected epochs, or never stopping at all), check whether the stopping-rule code itself is doing what its own parameters claim before concluding the budget needs to grow to match – the real fix here was one < becoming < ... - tolerance, not a bigger epoch budget.
  • **Real production bug found after an actual 50-replicate/8-alpha (3200-job) recovery-sweep deployment: 79% of condor_recovery_fit.R‘s companion *_history.csv diagnostic files came back empty, uniformly across every fitting alpha (79.2-79.8%), while every main result file was intact.** Root cause: submit_jobs_with_retry() (in condor_recovery_sweep_workflow.py) only ever validated output_col (the main result CSV) before deciding a job succeeded – the same file-transfer-overload issue this function exists to catch (see the condor_group_diff_workflow.py entry above) was still silently destroying the history file specifically, just never detected or retried, since nothing checked it. Fixed by adding an extra_outputs(job) parameter (a function returning additional paths that must also exist and be non-empty) and passing a lambda from run_fit_stage() computing the history path via a new history_output_name() helper (mirroring condor_recovery_fit.R’s own sub("\\.csv$", "_history.csv", ...) naming) – a failing extra output now retries the whole job, since a fresh Rscript run regenerates both files together. Default behavior (no extra_outputs) is unchanged, so the other three workflows’ own copies of this function are unaffected – consistent with this directory’s self-contained-per-workflow convention.
    • Used the surviving 21% of history files to investigate two follow-up questions, each informative in a different way. (1) Among capped (non-converged) rows with a usable history file, the patience counter was at a median of only 28% of tol_window when training was cut off – most capped runs were not on the verge of stopping, consistent with these being genuinely slow-converging fits rather than ones that just missed the cutoff by a hair. A small number of specific cells (gen alpha = 20 or Inf, crossed with low-to-moderate fitting alphas) showed hundreds to 1000+ genuine small improvements across the full 120000 epochs – a noisier, slower convergence regime than lower-generating-alpha cells, with gap-growth extrapolation projecting some of these would need ~125000-151000 epochs to genuinely converge. (2) Replaying the exact early-stopping rule against the same saved histories at a larger tolerance (analyze_recovery_history.py, already in this directory) showed all 144 previously-capped rows would have triggered genuine early stopping well within the recorded 120000-epoch trajectory at tolerance=5e-4 or 1e-3 (median stop epoch 59580 / 38235) – but at a real cost: mean loss given up relative to the best loss ever seen jumped from ~0.00005 (at the actual tolerance=1e-4) to 0.006-0.018, a 100-400x increase, risking reintroducing cross-cell quality differences via premature stopping rather than via hitting the epoch cap. Decided against raising tolerance sweep-wide for this reason: the point of the whole exercise was making sure the matched-vs-mismatched comparison wasn’t contaminated by some cells being less-converged than others, and a looser tolerance doesn’t actually guarantee that, just changes the mechanism.
    • condor_recovery_sweep_refit_capped.py (new companion script, + test_condor_recovery_sweep_refit_capped.py) – built instead, to re-fit only the cells that hit a prior run’s epoch ceiling without converging, at a higher max_epochs, rather than either leaving the comparison contaminated or re-running the entire sweep. Infers which cells were capped directly from the data (the largest epoch value anywhere in results_long.csv is the original ceiling; any row at or within one epoch of it counts as capped) rather than requiring the old ceiling to be re-typed by hand. Reuses the original run’s already-simulated stage0_simulate/ ground truth/triplets as-is (no resimulation) and re-derives each capped cell’s exact original fit_seed from its (replicate, generating alpha, fitting alpha) position using the identical formula run_fit_stage() itself uses (confirmed identical via a regression test that runs both code paths on the same synthetic config and compares the seed directly, not just re-implements the formula and trusts it matches) – so a refit cell retraces the same initialization/train-test split as its original attempt, just given room to actually reach its stopping criterion, making the result a legitimate like-for-like replacement rather than a different sample. Writes to a new stage_refit/ directory and new results_long_refit.csv/error_matrix_mean_refit.csv/error_matrix_sd_refit.csv – every row from the original dataset, with just the previously-capped ones replaced – leaving the original outputs untouched for comparison/provenance. Considered (and rejected, see above) re-running the whole sweep with a looser tolerance instead; the targeted refit also costs less total compute, since it only touches the ~21% of cells that actually needed it rather than redoing everything.
  • condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py (+ condor_joint_manifold_fit.R, condor_joint_manifold_update.R, joint_manifold_params_template.yml, README_joint_manifold.md, test_condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py) – fourth Condor workflow, the Condor-scale version of the “fully rigorous” (embedding-refit) joint geometry+choice-model manifold idea, validated locally on real Gabor Experiment 3 data via a decisive LOO comparison against the already-in-production baseline (each person’s own individual embedding, standard shared alpha=1): the rigorous model won on held-out validation-trial log-likelihood (20/24 participants, paired t-test p=0.0011) with a supportive but non-significant accuracy trend (16/24, p=0.14) – exactly the asymmetry expected for a model whose advantage is in choice-model calibration rather than in flipping which option gets predicted, since accuracy is structurally insensitive to alpha for this Student-t/crowd-kernel family (whichever option has the smaller distance always has higher predicted probability, for any alpha). That result (plus the recovered manifold position independently tracking the known contrast-vs-orientation axis in Experiment 3) was judged sufficient evidence to justify the Condor investment, scoped in a planning exchange before any code was written. Architecture: restructured from the naive “loop over folds, and within each fold loop over outer iterations” shape (which would pay Condor’s submission/queueing latency n_folds x n_outer times) to loop over outer iterations as the only sequential axis, submitting one Condor batch per iteration covering every participant’s refit at once. condor_joint_manifold_fit.R is the second workflow here (after the recovery sweep) to bypass train_embedding()’s CKL-only R wrapper via _fit_offline()-through-reticulate, warm-started from each participant’s current embedding (their original CrowdKernel fit on iteration 1, their own previous iteration’s refit after that) rather than random-noise initialization, which is why later iterations converge faster than the first (confirmed directly during local validation). condor_joint_manifold_update.R is new relative to every other workflow in this directory, but not in where it runs – it was originally built to run as a local Rscript call on the submit node (cheap, seconds, so another Condor round-trip seemed not worth it), but real-deployment feedback before the first actual test run found the submit node had no R installation and uncertain permissions to add one, so it was moved into its own single-job Condor batch per outer iteration, same container image as the refit jobs (which already has R + tripletTools) – restoring the “no R needed on the submit node” property every other workflow here has. Two real bugs caught during implementation, both before any Condor deployment: (1) the per-job embedding-refit output was initially going to be written under the same filename convention (person{i}.csv) as its own --init_embedding input, which would have collided within a single job’s transfer sandbox (the same direction of mistake condor_workflow.py’s own transfer-path-vs-argument-basename lesson warns about, just mirrored) – caught by manually tracing the file-naming chain across iterations before testing, not by a failing test; fixed by writing refit output under a distinct embedding_person{i}.csv name and renaming to person{i}.csv locally (zero-cost) once the whole batch completes. (2) the SAME class of collision resurfaced when the update step moved into Condor: its own --old_positions input would otherwise transfer in under the same name (positions.csv) its --output_positions writes out – fixed by staging the previous iteration’s positions file under a distinct old_positions_input.csv name before transfer. Validated short of an actual cluster deployment: 22 Python unit tests covering CSV validation, canonical item-order consistency checking, per-person train/test/pooled-trial file prep (zero-based indices, correct sampleSet split, graceful handling of a participant with no random trials), submit_jobs_with_retry() (copied in, same self-contained-per-workflow convention as the other three), and the update step’s Condor submit-file construction/output parsing (via a mocked subprocess.run standing in for condor_submit/condor_wait, no real cluster or Rscript needed) – plus a standalone functional smoke test of condor_joint_manifold_update.R itself (run directly, not through the orchestrator) against synthetic circular-embedding data with a built-in noise gradient, confirming the GPA/cmdscale/profiled-search pipeline runs end-to-end and recovers a position that correlates with the known gradient (r=-0.73). (The condor_recovery_fit.R seed bug found and fixed alongside this workflow’s first version is covered in its own entry below.) Only mode: fit (one joint estimate, no held-out evaluation) is implemented; mode: loo (the full leave-one-out validation mirroring the local decisive test) and run-resume support are both explicitly planned follow-ups, not yet built.
  • Found, while writing condor_joint_manifold_fit.R above, that condor_recovery_fit.R has had the exact same “seed never actually controlled a fit” bug already fixed once elsewhere in this project (see the run_embeddings_from_list()/run_group_embedding_from_list() entry earlier in this file): it calls _fit_offline() with random_state = NULL rather than the actual seed value, so two jobs with identical --seed only share an initial embedding and train/test split (both R-side, both correctly seeded) – the optimizer’s own internal randomness during gradient descent is never pinned down, so exact reruns aren’t bit-reproducible. Assessed as a reproducibility issue, not a validity one, for the recovery-sweep conclusions already drawn from it: those were established via replication across 20-50 independent ground-truth draws specifically so that run-to-run variability from any source gets absorbed into the between-replicate spread the significance tests already account for, the bug introduces unbiased per-job noise (fresh process per Condor job, no shared state to bias a particular direction), and if anything extra uncontrolled noise should make a true effect harder, not easier, to find significant – so the upper/lower-triangle asymmetry finding surviving replication despite this is mildly reassuring rather than undermined. No re-run of the existing sweep was judged necessary. Fixed by changing random_state = NULL to random_state = seed (one line), matching the already-established, working pattern.
  • Real deployment crash on condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py’s actual first submit-node run (Gabor Experiment 3 data): build_canonical_items() crashed prep_person_files() with AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'keys'. Root cause: build_canonical_items()’s by_worker dict was built via by_worker.setdefault(row["worker_id"], []).append(row["item"]) – appending just the item-name string, not the row – while prep_person_files() (its only caller) does by_item = {r["item"]: r for r in embedding_rows_by_worker[w]}, expecting each entry to be a full row dict with dim_* columns. No test caught this before the real run because every existing test exercised the two functions in isolation, each with hand-built inputs already in the shape the other function expects – the actual handoff between them (raw CSV rows all the way through to per-person embedding files) was never exercised end-to-end. Fixed by appending the full row instead of row["item"] (and deriving first_items from r["item"] for each row), plus a new end-to-end test chaining build_canonical_items() into prep_person_files() from raw rows, and a strengthened assertion on the existing unit test checking row shape (a dict with dim_0 present), not just count – both confirmed to fail against the reverted bug and pass against the fix before committing. General lesson, worth remembering for this directory’s other orchestrators too: testing each pure function in isolation with inputs shaped exactly as its signature implies does not exercise whether an upstream function’s actual output matches that shape – that only shows up in an integration test spanning the real call chain, which is why this one was worth adding even though it covers no new branch of either function individually.
  • Second real deployment failure on condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py’s first run, right after the previous one was fixed: every embedding-refit job failed with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pandas', after a telltale log of reticulate downloading uv, a fresh cpython-3.13 interpreter, and bare numpy from scratch. Root cause, confirmed directly against R/zzz.R: the "triplet-embeddings" conda environment is activated by reticulate::use_condaenv() inside tripletTools’s own .onLoad() – which only runs if the package is actually library()-loaded, not merely referenced via system.file(..., package = "tripletTools"). condor_joint_manifold_fit.R never called library(tripletTools), so .onLoad() never ran, so reticulate had no configured Python at all and fell back to auto-bootstrapping its own empty one via uv (a newer-reticulate fallback behavior) instead of finding the container’s real environment with torch/pandas/etc. already installed. Every other per-job fit script in this directory (condor_recovery_fit.R, condor_fit.R, condor_group_fit.R, condor_individual_fit.R) already calls library(tripletTools) for exactly this reason – confirmed by checking all four directly, not assumed – this new script was simply the one place that line was missing. Fixed by adding the same suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tripletTools)) call used everywhere else in this directory.
  • condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py documented in condor_workflows_vignette.Rmd as a new “Workflow 4” section (plus a new row in the Overview table, and a correction to “three independent workflows” -> “several,” since the recovery sweep was already a pre-existing fourth/fifth workflow with no vignette section of its own – a gap this pass did not attempt to backfill, flagged rather than silently worked around). Covers why the workflow exists (the decisive log-likelihood validation on Gabor Experiment 3, summarized briefly with a pointer to the full write-up living outside the package in the lab’s own research documentation), why it’s iterative unlike Workflows 1-3, and the update-step-moved-into-Condor design decision. The full scientific write-up itself was added as a new section, “Does jointly estimating geometry and choice model improve prediction?”, in the lab’s own triplet_choice_and_loss.Rmd (outside this package, in Simulation/ChoiceModels/) – extending the existing “Variation in choice model vs geometry” section’s open question with the Experiment 3 decisive result (20/24 participants, paired t=3.74t=3.74, p=0.0011p=0.0011 on held-out validation logLik), a live-computed sanity check that the recovered LOO positions correlate with an independent, previously-documented contrast-vs-orientation individual-difference axis (r=−0.593r=-0.593, p=0.0022p=0.0022, recomputed directly from the decisive run’s own per-participant output rather than reused from an earlier pilot), and a direct contrast with Experiment 1’s null result from the cheaper, embeddings-fixed version of the same check. Both documents verified by actually knitting them (not just inspecting source) and checking rendered numbers against the source computation.
  • condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py’s own real first deployment (30 participants, n_outer=2, mode: fit) completed cleanly – 60/60 refit jobs with empty .err files, stable beta0/beta1/positions across iterations, correctly-renamed embedding files – but its update-step output was missing the aligned/ directory, even though update.err was empty both iterations. Root cause, confirmed directly from the actual deployed update.sub the user pasted back: no explicit transfer_output_files was set, and HTCondor’s default “send back whatever’s new in the sandbox” output transfer reliably picks up new plain files (positions.csv/beta.csv came back fine) but does not reliably recurse into a newly-created subdirectory without naming it explicitly – a known HTCondor behavior, not a bug in condor_joint_manifold_update.R. Inconsequential for mode: fit (aligned_dir is write-only there, never read back downstream), but would matter for the still-unbuilt mode: loo. Fixed by adding an optional transfer_output_files parameter to write_submit_file() (left unset for the embedding-refit jobs, which only ever produce flat files) and passing "positions.csv, beta.csv, aligned" explicitly from the update step’s own submit-file call.
  • condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py gained resume support, motivated directly by its own first real production run (24 participants, n_outer=8). That run’s per-iteration beta0/beta1 trajectory looked concerning at first (still growing, not decelerating) but turned out to have a real, specific explanation once the per-participant position trajectories were pulled apart: most of the sample had converged by iteration 6, but a coherent subgroup of 6 participants had overshot to an extreme position around iterations 3-5 and were still steadily correcting back at iteration 8 (changes of 0.05-0.07 between iterations 6 and 8, vs <0.005 for the converged majority) – the global curve was still catching up to their correction, not diverging. (Bandwidth narrowing across the same iterations, initially also flagged as a possible overfitting signature, turned out to be roughly proportionate to a genuine, modest narrowing in the position distribution itself – checked directly via the bandwidth-to-SD ratio, which stayed near-constant rather than shrinking independently.) Since the orchestrator had no way to continue past a finished run other than restarting from iteration 1, extending this specific run to let that subgroup settle meant discarding 8 iterations of real compute. Fixed by making n_outer a total-iteration target rather than a fixed count: rerunning the same command (same output_dir) now auto-resumes after the last iteration with all expected outputs present (iterN/positions.csv, iterN/beta.csv, every iterN/refit/embeddings/person{i}.csv) rather than restarting, so raising n_outer and rerunning is how a run gets extended. Guards against the one real correctness risk this introduces – a resume silently using a different triplet_data.csv/embeddings.csv than the original run, which would misattribute every person{i}.csv-indexed position/embedding to the wrong participant – by recording the exact worker_id order and item order the first time setup/ is built (setup/worker_ids.txt, setup/item_order.txt) and refusing to resume (clear error, not a silent mismatch) if a later invocation’s inputs would produce a different order. A new --fresh flag forces starting over regardless. 15 new unit tests (37 total) cover the resume-point scan (including that an incomplete iteration in the middle of a run is correctly treated as the resume point, not skipped over in favor of a later-looking-complete one from some earlier abandoned attempt) and the id-consistency check in both directions.
  • Real finding from the first genuine production run (24 participants, extended via resume to n_outer=30): final_embeddings.csv (each participant’s own individually-refit embedding) showed a clean, monotonic, textbook overfitting signature against the baseline – a validation-logLik comparison against each person’s own plain individual embedding (standard shared alpha=1) was marginally positive at iteration 1 (+0.16, not significant) and degraded smoothly and monotonically to significantly negative by iteration 30 (-4.32, p=0.0068), with implied alpha spanning 0.007 to 3.3 million across participants by the end. This looked like a direct contradiction of the earlier decisive LOO validation (+3.19, p=0.0011) until the actual discrepancy was found: that LOO test never evaluated a held-out participant’s own refit embedding at all – it evaluated the kernel-smoothed pooled estimate (embed_at(): a weighted average across the whole aligned pool at that participant’s own recovered position), since in the LOO design the held-out person’s own embedding was excluded from the pool entirely. Re-running the SAME overfitting check using that correct estimator (recomputing GPA alignment locally from each iteration’s own refit embeddings, so every iteration could be checked without needing the aligned/ output specifically) showed no overfitting trend at all – the smoothed estimate beat the baseline at every iteration from 1 to 30, strongest early, dipping modestly through the middle (while positions were still settling), and re-strengthening and stabilizing from iteration ~22 onward almost exactly when the late position flips (see the resume-support entry above) resolved. The individually-refit embedding (the workflow’s own main output) was never the validated artifact – the kernel-smoothed pooled estimate was, and the two can diverge sharply as a person’s own alpha becomes extreme. Fixed by adding final_smoothed_embeddings.csv/final_smoothed_alpha.csv as proper workflow outputs (write_smoothed_outputs()), computed via a pure-Python reimplementation of embed_at() plus an exact reimplementation of R’s stats::bw.nrd0() (verified bit-for-bit against a real R reference value – an approximate bandwidth formula would silently use a different kernel than the one the R-side update step actually validated against). Requires the final iteration’s aligned/ output (the thing the transfer_output_files fix a few entries up made reliable); skips with a printed note, not a failure, if it’s missing. 9 new tests (46 total).
  • Full 30-participant Experiment 3 production run, plus a real methodological question from the user that led to a genuinely useful decomposition. With resume support, n_outer=30 was run on all 30 available Experiment 3 participants (not just the 24-participant quality-gated subset); the earlier 24- and 30-participant runs were moved to GaborTriplets/joint_manifolds/condor_joint_manifold_output_ex3{,_n24} to make room (see the directory-collision note below). The full-sample production comparison strengthened rather than weakened relative to n=24 (25/30 win, mean diff +3.00 nats, p=0.000118p=0.000118) and surfaced a second real non-convergence case distinct from the resume-support one: worker 95061’s position genuinely oscillates between two states across all 30 iterations (amplitude ~0.3, still moving 0.35 at the final transition) rather than converging, landing by coincidence within 0.0001 of a different worker’s own genuinely-converged final position – caught by plotting the full trajectory, not trusting the final-iteration number. Separately, the full-sample run’s choice-model curve was dramatically more moderate than the 24-participant subset’s (beta1 1.76 vs. 14.56) – checked whether the six additional participants simply filled previously-sparse territory (they don’t; their positions overlap the original 24’s own range) and reported this as a plausible-but-unconfirmed curve-fitting-stability account rather than a proven mechanism.
    • The user then asked a sharp methodological question: since every participant’s own data informs both their own refit and the shared curve, is the production comparison’s win just self-contribution, or could it even be explained away – if there were no real shared structure, shouldn’t pooling in other participants’ data make a held-out prediction worse, not better, by the user’s own correct bias-variance argument? This was answered empirically, not rhetorically, with a controlled decomposition: four conditions (own vs. pooled/kernel-smoothed embedding) x (alpha fixed at 1 vs. the fitted smoothed-alpha curve). Alpha-smoothing alone, embedding held at each participant’s own refit, does nothing (p=0.597p=0.597) – unsurprising, since accuracy is structurally alpha-invariant for this choice-model family and logLik barely moved either. Embedding-pooling alone, alpha held fixed at 1 – the clean test of the user’s question – is itself a clear win (23/30, mean diff +2.06 nats, p=0.0018p=0.0018), ruling out both the alpha-recalibration confound and (by the user’s own correct logic) the no-real-structure account. A second, fully independent check followed immediately: loo_trajectory_accuracy() (already existing, no Condor run needed, no alpha component at all, full participant exclusion including from the 1-D axis itself) gave R² = 0.72, p=2.6×10−9p=2.6\times10^{-9} on the same n=30 data – about as decisive as this kind of test gets. Both pieces of evidence, plus the original small-scale full-refit LOO (p=0.0011p=0.0011), are documented in triplet_choice_and_loss.Rmd’s new “Is the embedding-pooling advantage real, or an artifact?” section, which closes with a concrete recommendation for future datasets: these two cheap checks (no Condor needed) answer the existence question, and the expensive mode: loo Condor workflow (one full production run per held-out participant) is worth its cost only when the magnitude of benefit to a genuinely new participant specifically needs to be trustworthy – a headline effect size, or sizing a real application – not as a routine step on every new dataset.
    • A real near-miss, not a data-loss incident: between sessions, the user ran the same workflow on Experiment 1 data (orientation-only Gabors, 38 participants, d=2d=2) using the default condor_joint_manifold_output output directory – the same path the Experiment 3 n=30 run had used – which would have silently overwritten the n=30 run’s raw per-iteration data (the thing triplet_choice_and_loss.Rmd’s oscillation-trajectory figure reads directly from disk at knit time) had the user not already moved the prior results to joint_manifolds/condor_joint_manifold_output_ex3{,_n24} first. Caught via the harness’s own file-change notification on iter30/beta.csv, confirmed via run_manifest.txt showing the Experiment 1 inputs at that path, and resolved by updating the one Rmd chunk that reads the live directory (cj_dir) to the new joint_manifolds/... path.
