Worth remembering generally: this project’s established convention of appending a suffix to a prior run’s output directory (_n24, now _ex3) only protects against collision if it happens before the next run starts, not after – there is no in-workflow safeguard against two different datasets being pointed at the same default output path.
  • summarize_joint_estimation() (new) – the user, now having run this workflow on a second dataset (Experiment 1) and anticipating several more, asked for the diagnostics generated by hand above (convergence checking, individual-vs-smoothed comparison) to become a reusable function rather than a repeated manual exercise. Reads a condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py output directory directly (run_manifest.txt, setup/worker_ids.txt/item_order.txt, every iterN/positions.csv/beta.csv, setup/original_embeddings/, final_embeddings.csv, final_smoothed_embeddings.csv/final_smoothed_alpha.csv when present) and writes a self-contained Markdown report (figures as sibling PNGs, relative links) covering position-convergence flagging, the beta/bandwidth trajectory, the choice-model curve, and a 2-D/3-D embedding-geometry grid – all of this needs nothing beyond output_dir itself. The held-out validation comparison (the four-way decomposition from the discussion above, plus the loo_trajectory_accuracy() confirmation) is gated on an optional triplet_data argument, since validation trials are deliberately never passed to the Condor workflow at all (assign_sample_sets()’s "holdout" convention) and so cannot be recovered from output_dir alone – the original baseline embeddings, by contrast, are already saved under setup/original_embeddings/ and need no separate argument. Reuses already-exported package functions (generalized_procrustes() and smooth_embedding_trajectory() via its explicit query_points argument, get.rep.dist(), loo_trajectory_accuracy()) rather than re-deriving kernel-smoothing/GPA logic a second time; the profiled Student-t/crowd-kernel likelihood machinery, needed for the decomposition and not available anywhere else in the package (only duplicated across the standalone Condor R scripts, which are deliberately self-contained for cluster deployment – a rationale that doesn’t apply here, since this lives inside the package itself), is factored into one proper internal helper (ckl_validation_eval()) instead of being duplicated a fourth time. Verified against real data, not just a synthetic fixture: run on the actual Experiment 3 n=30 output directory, every number in the generated report (the decomposition table, the flagged-participant table, the LOO R²) matched the hand-computed analysis above exactly; run on the actual Experiment 1 output directory with no triplet_data (confirming graceful skipping of the comparison sections) and surfaced a second, independently real non-convergence case worth noting for its own sake – a different worker whose position converges smoothly for 29 iterations and then jumps sharply at the very last one, a distinct failure mode from worker 95061’s sustained oscillation above, caught by the same flagging logic without any manual trajectory inspection. p_acc is reported as NA (not a bug) whenever two compared conditions share the same embedding and differ only in alpha, since R’s own t.test() returns NA (not an error) for an exactly-zero-variance paired difference – documented with a footnote in the generated report rather than left to look like a silent failure. New test file test-summarize_joint_estimation.R (21 assertions) builds a small synthetic fake output directory (geometric position convergence, one engineered last-iteration jump) covering both the self-contained diagnostics and, separately, the triplet_data-gated comparison/LOO path.
  • Run live on Experiment 1 with real triplet_data for the first time, and a chain of real methodological questions that fully resolved a genuine open tension. The decomposition showed a strong embedding-pooling win for Experiment 1 too (32/38, p=2.8×10−7p=2.8\times10^{-7}) – on its face in tension with the fully out-of-sample loo_trajectory_accuracy() null (R²=0.02, p=0.38p=0.38) documented above. Resolved in stages, each tested rather than argued: (1) isolating the refit procedure itself from pooling (own refit, unpooled, vs. original: p=0.88p=0.88, nothing) ruled out “refitting is just better optimization”; (2) comparing the position-weighted pooled estimate against a plain, position-independent grand mean (same embedding for everyone) showed the grand mean alone already recovers the entire effect (30/38 win on its own, p=1.7×10−6p=1.7\times10^{-6}) and position-weighting adds nothing on top (23/38, p=0.53p=0.53) – the win is pure noise reduction from averaging, not anything about where a given participant specifically sits in the pool; (3) directly checking the grand mean against the known orientation ground-truth circle (same construction as triplet_choice_and_loss.Rmd’s circular-geometry analysis) found a Procrustes correlation of 0.988 – far exceeding even the single best individual embedding’s own fidelity (max 0.926, median 0.745) – confirming the grand mean isn’t just a consensus, it recovers the true geometry almost exactly, which is exactly why pooling helps despite there being no real cross-participant manifold; (4) this in turn explains the Rmd’s own documented alpha-vs-circular-fidelity correlation as largely an estimation-precision artifact (lower alpha -> noisier decisions -> noisier individual embedding estimate of the same true circle, not a different true geometry), fully compatible with pooling denoising it away. One follow-up test came out negative, which was itself informative: the ~8 participants whose own individual embedding beats the true circle on their own held-out trials (geom_mismatch in the Rmd) were tested for whether they share a common alternative geometry with each other – pairwise Procrustes distance among them is statistically indistinguishable from a random same-size subset (permutation p=0.77p=0.77), and a leave-one-out subgroup mean built from just the other outliers is the worst of four predictors tested (0.598 mean accuracy, behind even the generic circle’s 0.600 and the full-population grand mean’s 0.625) – these participants are idiosyncratically different from everyone, including each other, not a coherent second cluster, so no pooling scheme (subgroup or population-wide) has anything to offer them specifically.
  • Grand mean added as a first-class output, both in the Condor workflow and in summarize_joint_estimation()’s report, directly motivated by the resolution above. write_smoothed_outputs() (condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py) now also computes and writes final_grand_mean_embedding.csv (grand_mean_embedding(), pure unweighted average across the final iteration’s aligned pool, no kernel weighting) alongside the existing smoothed outputs – same aligned/ input already being read, so effectively free. 2 new Python unit tests (48 total). summarize_joint_estimation()’s decomposition grew from 5 to 7 rows: (e) grand mean vs. (a) baseline and (c) position-weighted pool vs. (e) grand mean, the latter being the direct test of “does a participant’s own recovered position add anything beyond plain averaging.” Reads final_grand_mean_embedding.csv when present (same graceful-fallback-to-local-recomputation pattern as final_smoothed_*, via generalized_procrustes() on final_embeddings). Re-run on both real datasets to confirm the asymmetry predicted before writing any code: Experiment 1’s grand mean beats baseline decisively (30/38, p=1.7×10−6p=1.7\times10^{-6}) with position adding nothing (p=0.53p=0.53); Experiment 3’s grand mean does not reliably beat baseline at all (17/30, p=0.70p=0.70, slightly negative), while position-weighting on top of it is itself significant (22/30, mean diff +2.43 nats, p=0.0080p=0.0080) – exactly the opposite pattern, confirming the comparison correctly distinguishes a dataset with real manifold structure from one without. Also fixed an unrelated latent bug surfaced while touching the test file: build_fake_jm_output()’s synthetic per-person embeddings used unseeded rnorm() jitter, making the test suite genuinely flaky (one run hit a degenerate LOO fold and errored inside get.hoacc()) – fixed with an explicit set.seed(), confirmed by rerunning the suite multiple times after the fix with no recurrence.
  • condor_workflows_vignette.Rmd’s “Workflow 4” section brought up to date rather than spinning off a new vignette – summarize_joint_estimation() is a companion tool to this exact workflow, and this package’s convention is to extend a thematically-related vignette rather than fragment into many small ones. The section had gone stale in ways that were actively misleading, not just incomplete, by the time this was done: it still pointed readers at final_embeddings.csv/final_positions.csv with no warning, even though that’s precisely the artifact the overfitting-misdiagnosis finding above showed is not safe to use; its outputs table predated final_smoothed_embeddings.csv/final_smoothed_alpha.csv/final_grand_mean_embedding.csv/aligned/ entirely; it said nothing about resume support; and “mode: loo is a planned follow-up” no longer matched the actual, now-settled position (deliberately deprioritized in favor of two cheap checks, build only if a magnitude claim specifically needs it – see the triplet_choice_and_loss.Rmd entry above). Fixed all four, and added a new “Summarizing and interpreting a run” subsection demonstrating summarize_joint_estimation() itself, including a worked summary of the real cross-dataset asymmetry (grand mean alone explains Experiment 1’s pooling benefit, p=0.53p=0.53 for position on top of it; Experiment 3’s needs real position-weighting, p=0.0080p=0.0080) as the motivating example for why the decomposition table exists at all. Verified by actually knitting the vignette (knitr::knit(), 33/33 chunks; full HTML render via rmarkdown::render() wasn’t possible in this environment – no pandoc installed – so this is Markdown-level verification only, same limitation as any other render in this environment, not specific to this change) rather than just checking the source looked right.
  • condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py redesigned: alpha is now decoupled from geometric position by default, not a function of it. Direct continuation of the investigation above – the user asked whether there was any actual rationale (computational or otherwise) for tying alpha to geometry, given the decoupled-with-proper-regularization design had just been shown to tie with the coupled one on the dataset where coupling mattered and to avoid a real liability on the other. No such rationale survived: the only genuine advantage of coupling was getting alpha’s regularization “for free” from machinery already needed for geometry, which is moot once the decoupled machinery is already built and validated (as it now was); the robustness argument (coupling can’t run away to a degenerate per-person estimate the way an unconstrained per-person alpha fit can) turned out to be an argument for some regularization, not for coupling specifically, since the decoupled-with-shrinkage version handles the exact same failure mode just as well. For the eventual paper, decoupled is also the easier story: “each participant’s alpha gets standard empirical-Bayes partial pooling, independent of geometry” needs no special justification, where “alpha is tied to the same manifold position as geometry” is the assumption that needed defending and didn’t hold up.
    • condor_joint_manifold_update.R rewritten: step 3 (position search) now scores candidate positions at each participant’s own fixed current alpha rather than a curve evaluated at the candidate position; step 4 no longer refits a shared 2-parameter curve (beta0/beta1) – it re-estimates each participant’s own alpha directly, via a per-person profiled MLE over the same bounded grid used throughout this investigation (10^seq(log10(2e-4), log10(2e6), length.out = 140) – avoids the unconstrained-optimizer runaway confirmed for participants whose own data is highly self-consistent, some individual estimates diverged past 101010^{10} without a bound) followed by empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward a precision-weighted population mean (a standard random-effects DerSimonian-Laird estimator of the between-person variance net of estimation noise). The precision-weighting specifically matters: an initial, simpler unweighted shrinkage estimator was tried first and collapsed to zero between-person variance on both validation datasets, traced to a handful of poorly-identified (near-boundary) individuals distorting the variance estimate as much as well-identified ones – the precision-weighted DerSimonian-Laird version doesn’t have this problem, confirmed directly against both real datasets (τ² came out clearly nonzero, 0.124 and 1.172, where the naive estimator gave exactly 0 for both). --old_beta0/--old_beta1 replaced by --old_alpha (a staged file path, same old_positions_input.csv-style distinct-name convention, not a command-line scalar, since it’s now one value per pool member); output is alpha.csv (one row per pool member: log_alpha, alpha, log_alpha_raw, se_log_alpha, shrinkage_weight per-person, plus tau2/pop_mean_alpha/bandwidth repeated globally) replacing beta.csv. Smoke-tested standalone against synthetic circular-embedding data (same established pattern as the script’s original validation) in two passes: an initial version using a deterministic “closer-to-truth-wins” choice rule produced near-saturated likelihoods (alpha pinned near the grid boundary for nearly everyone, bandwidth collapsed near zero) – not a code bug, a test-data artifact (zero simulated decision noise), fixed by generating choices probabilistically via the actual crowd-kernel rule against each participant’s own noisy embedding instead; the corrected version produced sensible position spread, a non-degenerate bandwidth, a believable mix of well- and poorly-identified (boundary-pinned) alpha estimates with shrinkage visibly pulling the latter back toward the population – and a second run confirmed the --old_positions/--old_alpha resume-staging path also works.
    • condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py updated to match: the main iteration loop no longer computes alphas = [exp(beta0 + beta1*position) ...] each round – it just passes through whatever alphas the previous iteration’s update step (or find_resume_state(), on a resume) already returned, since alpha is a direct per-person value now, not derived from a curve. write_smoothed_outputs() no longer computes or writes an alpha file at all (nothing position-dependent left to compute); final_alpha.csv is written directly in main() from the per-person values already in memory. run_manifest.txt reports alpha estimation: decoupled... and a final mean alpha instead of final beta0/beta1. The module-level docstring and condor_joint_manifold_fit.R’s own --alpha argument comment were both rewritten to describe the new design (the docstring was also stale on an unrelated point found in passing – it still said the update step “runs as a LOCAL Rscript call on the submit node,” which stopped being true when that step was moved into Condor in an earlier session; fixed as part of this same pass). 2 new Python unit tests (49 total) plus substantial rewrites to TestRunUpdateStep/TestIterationIsComplete/TestFindResumeState/TestWriteSmoothedOutputs for the new alpha.csv-based signatures.
    • summarize_joint_estimation() updated in step: read_joint_manifold_run() now builds an alpha_mat (n participants x n_outer, mirroring positions_mat) and a small alpha_diag_traj (per-iteration tau2/pop_mean_alpha/bandwidth) from each iteration’s alpha.csv, instead of a single beta_traj; reads final_alpha.csv (renamed from final_smoothed_alpha.csv, now a direct per-person pass-through with no position dependence). New flag_unstable_joint_alpha() gives alpha its own independent convergence check (log-alpha space, same window/threshold convention as position’s). The “Choice-model curve across the manifold” report section (a fitted alpha(t) line, which no longer exists) is replaced by a purely descriptive final-alpha-vs-position scatter plot that assumes no relationship. Real bug caught before this shipped, found by running the updated function against a real old-format run (predates this redesign, so it has no iterN/alpha.csv or final_alpha.csv at all): graphics::matplot() on an all-NA alpha_mat (log10(NA) throughout) failed with “need finite ‘ylim’ values,” an unhandled crash rather than a graceful skip. Fixed with a has_alpha_traj <- !all(is.na(run$alpha_mat)) guard around both new alpha plots and the alpha-flagging table, printing an explanatory note instead – the same “skip gracefully, don’t fail the whole report” pattern write_smoothed_outputs()’s own missing-aligned/ handling already established, now applied to this new failure mode too. Verified end-to-end against that same real old-format directory after the fix: runs cleanly, correctly reports “no iterN/alpha.csv found… predates alpha being decoupled from position,” and the held-out comparison’s estimate_shrunk_alpha() fallback (triggered since final_alpha.csv doesn’t exist either) reproduced numbers consistent with the by-hand validation earlier in this investigation. Test fixture (build_fake_jm_output()) updated to write per-iteration alpha.csv (varying by worker, not constant – an initial constant-alpha version produced degenerate zero-variance paired differences once combined with the fixture’s already-identical toy embeddings/trials, triggering t.test()’s “data are essentially constant” error) and gained a new oscillate_alpha_last parameter, independent of oscillate_last (position), exercising the new independent alpha-convergence check; 33 assertions total (up from 24), including new direct tests of flag_unstable_joint_alpha() and estimate_shrunk_alpha().
    • Documentation: inst/condor/README_joint_manifold.md and vignettes/condor_workflows_vignette.Rmd’s Workflow 4 section both rewritten for the decoupled design – updated outputs tables (alpha.csv/final_alpha.csv replacing beta.csv/final_smoothed_alpha.csv), the iteration-steps description, the resume-state description, and a new subsection in each (Does alpha need to be tied to geometry? / the README’s own top-of-file note) explaining the finding and pointing to triplet_choice_and_loss.Rmd for the full comparison. Verified by re-knitting the vignette end-to-end (33/33 chunks, no errors).
  • Real production incident: a HELD Condor job stalled an overnight condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py deployment completely, with no automatic recovery. condor_q -held showed Error from slot1_11@e2472.chtc.wisc.edu: ... invalid mount config for type "bind": bind source path does not exist: /cvmfs – a transient broken Docker/CVMFS mount on one specific bad CHTC execute node, unrelated to the job’s own code, data, or container image. The real problem wasn’t the hold itself (a plain condor_release fixes it, since the matchmaker reassigns the job to a different slot rather than retrying the same bad one) – it’s that every orchestrator’s submit_and_wait() called a single blocking condor_wait with no timeout, and condor_wait only returns once every job in its log has terminated or been removed; a held job does neither until a human intervenes. So the driver’s blocking wait sat there all night with no way to notice or recover on its own, distinct from (and not covered by) submit_jobs_with_retry(), which only checks for missing/empty output after condor_wait already returned – it never fires if the wait itself never returns.
    • Fixed identically across all five orchestrators (condor_workflow.py, condor_group_diff_workflow.py, condor_individual_embeddings_workflow.py, condor_recovery_sweep_workflow.py, condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py – same self-contained-per-workflow duplication convention as every other shared fix here, e.g. submit_jobs_with_retry() itself): submit_and_wait() now parses the cluster id out of condor_submit‘s own stdout, then polls with condor_wait -wait 120 <log> in a loop instead of one open-ended call. On each timeout it checks condor_q <cluster> -held -af ProcId HoldReason and auto-releases (condor_release) anything found held, up to 3 releases per job before giving up with a clear error naming the job and its hold reason – rather than either hanging forever or failing instantly on a merely-transient hold. New HELD_JOB_MAX_RELEASES/HELD_JOB_POLL_SECONDS constants and a held_jobs_in_cluster() helper, duplicated into each file the same way. 4 new tests in test_condor_joint_manifold_workflow.py (53 total; all 93 tests across the other four workflows’ own suites pass unchanged, confirming the signature/behavior change – condor_wait now called with extra args, an occasional new condor_q/condor_release call – doesn’t break any existing mocked test, none of which asserted the exact condor_wait argument list, only cmd[0]). README_joint_manifold.md, README_group_diff.md, README_individual_embeddings.md, README_recovery_sweep.md, and condor_workflows_vignette.Rmd’s shared troubleshooting section (a new “A job goes held mid-run” subsection, mirroring the existing “empty output” one’s structure) all updated to describe the new auto-release behavior instead of telling the reader to notice and release a held job manually.
  • Real bug found in get.combined(): an all-digit worker_id column is silently read back as numeric, dropping leading zeros. Surfaced while helping the user add a write.csv() step to Simulation/ManifoldEstimation/ManifoldEstimation.Rmd (outside this package, a research notebook) so freshly-regenerated simulated triplets could round-trip through get.combined() without a stale CSV in between. simulate.participant()’s random 10-digit worker_id strings have about a 96% chance across 30 participants that at least one starts with 0; read.csv()’s default type inference reads an all-digit-looking column as numeric regardless, so e.g. "0733092758" came back as the numeric 733092758 – same root cause, same failure signature (IDs silently merged/dropped on mismatch) as the already-documented, already-fixed Python-side bug in compute_embeddings.py::process_all_workers() above, just independently present on the R/CSV-reading side of this shared, exported function. Confirmed directly: unique(tmp$worker_id) after a plain read.csv() showed several IDs 1-2 digits short of the expected 10. Fixed by forcing worker_id (and item, for the eflag=TRUE embeddings case, same risk in principle) to character via a targeted colClasses argument – reads the header first to build a named colClasses vector only for whichever of those two columns are actually present, leaving every other column’s type auto-detected as before. New regression test (test-get_combined.R) locks down the exact failure mode: a 2-participant synthetic CSV with one ID starting with 0, asserting the read-back ID stays a full 10-character string and its 2 rows aren’t split off into an unmatched, dangling entry. Full 241-block package test suite re-run and confirmed unaffected.
  • **summarize_joint_estimation()‘s embedding-geometry grid was silently double-smoothing, visibly flattening real structure.** Found after the user re-ran the decoupled-alpha workflow on Experiment 1 (GaborTriplets/joint_manifold_exp1, 38 participants, n_outer=30) and noticed the geometry-grid panels didn’t recover the known circular arrangement of the orientation stimuli nearly as cleanly as the original always-fit-at-alpha=1 individual embeddings did. Root cause: smoothed_source <- run$final_smoothed_embeddings %||% run$final_embeddings preferred the already-pooled/kernel-smoothed file (the same preference used correctly everywhere else in the report, since the raw per-person refit is the known-to-overfit artifact – see the “real finding” entry above), but the grid itself then calls smooth_embedding_trajectory() a second time on whatever it picked, to interpolate across a grid of query positions that generally aren’t any real participant’s actual position. When the smoothed file is present (every current-format run), that means smoothing twice with the same kernel/bandwidth – close to convolving a Gaussian with itself, which compounds to an effective bandwidth roughly sqrt(2)x larger than intended – over-flattening exactly the position-dependent geometric structure the plot exists to show. Fixed by always building the grid from the raw run$final_embeddings directly (renamed smoothed_source -> geometry_source), a single smoothing pass, matching the only case where this worked correctly before (an old-format run with no final_smoothed_embeddings.csv at all). Verified by re-rendering both real datasets’ reports: Experiment 1’s grid now shows a clean, well-formed ring with the orientation color gradient running smoothly around it from t=-0.15 onward, matching what the original per-individual alpha=1 fits recovered – the one remaining ragged panel (t=-0.59, the extreme low tail) is expected, not a smoothing artifact, since that’s the sparse-data boundary region where the one position-unstable participant (67e08871..., flagged in the same report’s convergence table) sits. All 33 existing tests pass unchanged (they only assert the PNG file is written, not its content). Purely a visualization fix – no statistics in the decomposition table or loo_trajectory_accuracy() check were ever affected, since neither reads final_smoothed_embeddings through this code path.
